ta-l1d4q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus opening Distinction 4. Having proved the Trinity by authorities, reasons, and likenesses, Lombard now takes up incidental questions. Since the persons are distinguished by procession, he first asks about procession with respect to its supposit and terminus (Dist. 4–5) and then with respect to its principle (Dist. 6, whether the Father begot by will or necessity). The same questions apply to the Spirit's procession. The first part asks whether concrete essential names can stand as supposit or terminus of generation ('God begot God'), and then (Dist. 5) whether abstract essential names can ('the Father begot the divine essence'). Personal names raise no doubt. Lombard argues for 'God begot God', resolves objections leading to absurdity, and refutes those who grant that the three persons are one God but deny that one God is three persons. Thomas announces two inquiries, on divine generation and on divine predication. The first has three articles: whether there is generation in God, whether 'God begot God' is true, and related locutions.
claims: The Trinity is distinguished by the procession of one person from another.
Concrete and abstract essential names differ in whether they can supposit for persons in notional propositions.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e124.summary: First objection against generation in God. Generation is a species of change (the Philosopher), and change is excluded from God (James 1:17).
claims: Generation is a species of change, and God is unchangeable.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e130.summary: Second objection. The nobler creatures are, the more they resemble God, and generation is found only in lower creatures, not in angels or heavenly bodies.
claims: Generation is absent from the noblest creatures.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e133.summary: Third objection. In any generation something is communicated from generator to generated, and by that the generated is not distinguished from the generator. Something else must distinguish them, so everything generated is composite. God has no composition, so there is no generation in him.
claims: Whatever is generated has something common and something distinguishing, and so is composite.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e137.summary: Fourth objection. Generation is an act intermediate between generator and generated, and nothing is intermediate between Father and Son.
claims: Generation is a medium between generator and generated.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e140.summary: Sed contra from Isaiah 66:9: shall I who give generation to others be barren?
claims: God, who gives generation, is not himself barren.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e145.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever communicates itself does so by reason of its act, since potency does not act. The divine essence is first and pure act and so communicates itself supremely. It does not do so in creatures, which do not receive the same nature, so it communicates itself through generation in the Son, the greatest communication.
claims: Act is the principle of self-communication, and pure act communicates itself supremely.
Supreme self-communication requires communication of the same nature.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e148.summary: Thomas's determination. That there is generation in God cannot be effectively proved by reason (Dist. 3) but is held by authority and faith. Since every perfection and no imperfection is in God, whatever is perfect in creatures can be said of him with imperfection removed. Names imposed from imperfection (stone, lion) are said of God metaphorically; names imposed from perfection are said properly, though eminently. A name is imposed from what functions as a constitutive difference, not from the genus. So when something implies imperfection by its genus and perfection by its difference, it is in God according to the difference. Knowledge, for example, is not in God as a habit or quality but as certain cognition. The genus of generation, change, implies passage from potency to act, materiality, and division of essence, none of which befits divine generation. Its difference implies perfection: passively, receiving an essence in perfect likeness; actively, communicating it. Communication follows on act and pertains to nobility. Generation so understood is in God first, and all creaturely generation descends from it and imitates it (Eph. 3:15). Taken in the ordinary sense used of creatures, it applies to God only by transference.
claims: Divine generation is held by faith and cannot be proved by reason.
Names are said properly of God when imposed from perfection, according to the constitutive difference, with the generic imperfection removed.
Generation, as communication of nature in perfect likeness, is found first in God; creaturely generation imitates it.
concepts: genus and difference in divine names

ta-l1d4q1-d1e154.summary: Reply to the first objection. Generation by its genus, change, is not in God. In God it is not change but an operation of the divine nature (Damascene). Operation differs from motion as the act of the perfect differs from the act of what exists in potency.
claims: Divine generation is an operation, the act of the perfect, not a motion.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e157.summary: Reply to the second objection. No creature can generate without imperfection. Since essence and being differ in every creature, an essence can be communicated to another supposit only under another being, so created essence is divided by communication, which is imperfect. That is why generation is absent from the most perfect creatures and present in those furthest from the divine likeness.
claims: Creaturely generation divides the essence because creaturely essence and esse differ.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e161.summary: Reply to the third objection. In divine generation nothing is added to the essence in the begotten by which it differs from the begetter. By receiving the essence it is distinguished by the relation of giver and receiver, and these relations differ from the essence only conceptually. So no composition follows. This is impossible in creatures, where no relation is really substance, so everything generated there is composite.
claims: The Son is distinguished from the Father only by the relation of receiving, not by anything added to the essence.
Divine relations are really identical with the essence, so divine generation implies no composition.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e164.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Generation is not really intermediate between Father and Son. Taken passively it is filiation, the Son's property in the Son; taken actively it is paternity in the Father, which is the Father. It signifies a property by way of an act, and this signification is grounded in reality in one person's receiving from another.
claims: Divine generation is really paternity (active) or filiation (passive), signified by way of act.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e176.summary: First objection that 'God begot God' is false. Generation implies a relation distinguishing the persons, so granting it would require granting that God is distinguished from God and is other than God, which is not granted.
claims: Begetting implies distinction between begetter and begotten.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e179.summary: Second objection. A predicate does not draw the subject term beyond its signification but only restricts it by tense; rather, predicates are such as their subjects allow (Boethius). 'God' signifies the essence, so it supposits for the essence, and 'essence begot essence' is false (Dist. 5).
claims: The predicate does not change the supposition of the subject term.
'God' signifies essence, and 'essence begot essence' is false.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e182.summary: Third objection. If God begot God, God is generating and generated. Whatever is said of each person can be said of God, so 'God generates' and 'God does not generate' would both be true, which is impossible.
claims: Predicates of individual persons transfer to 'God'.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e186.summary: Sed contra from the Creed: 'God from God, begotten'. One is begotten from God only as from a begetter, so God begets God.
claims: The Creed affirms 'God from God, begotten'.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e192.summary: Second sed contra. 'God' means one having deity, so whatever is said of one having deity can be said of God, and one having deity begets one having deity.
claims: 'God' signifies one having deity.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e195.summary: Thomas's determination: 'God begets God' is simply true. There are two opinions about why. One holds that 'God' signifies and of itself supposits for the essence but is drawn by a notional adjunct to supposit for a person, given the essence's indifference to the persons. The other, which Thomas judges truer, holds that 'God' signifies the essence but of itself supposits for a person indistinctly, so it can stand for one person ('God generates') or several ('God is Trinity'). Every name falls short of the divine being (Liber de causis): abstract names do not signify the subsistent, and concrete names signify the composite. Removing the imperfection, we use both, abstract names for simplicity and concrete names for perfection. 'God', like 'man', signifies by way of the perfect and subsistent and so includes the supposit indistinctly. It can supposit for a person of itself, and it supposits for the essence not by its mode of signifying but by divine simplicity, in which essence and supposit are really the same.
claims: 'God begets God' is simply true.
'Deus' signifies the essence but of itself supposits indistinctly for a person.
Abstract names are used of God for his simplicity, concrete names for his perfection.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e198.summary: Reply to the first objection. 'To beget' signifies a property by way of act, and acts belong only to supposits (humanity does not beget, a man does), so 'God begets God' is simply true. But 'to be related' and 'to be distinguished' signify acts only grammatically and can refer to essence or supposit. So 'God is distinguished from God' is not granted simply, lest the distinction be referred to the essence, especially since 'God' implies an indistinct supposit, distinguished only by an added personal property.
claims: Acts belong to supposits, so notional verbs make 'God' stand for a person.
'Distinguished' and 'related' are not acts and could be referred to the essence, so 'God is distinguished from God' is not granted.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e201.summary: Reply to the second objection. Although 'God' signifies the essence, of itself it supposits for one having the essence, a thing of the nature, even without considering the persons that faith distinguishes. It can supposit for a person without being restricted by anything else, and since it does so indistinctly it can stand for any person. In 'God begets God', the subject stands for the Father and the predicate term for the Son.
claims: In 'God begets God' the subject supposits for the Father and the predicate for the Son.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e204.summary: Reply to the third objection. 'God' is strictly neither universal nor singular. It is like a universal in being predicated essentially of several supposits, so what is predicated of each is predicated of it. It is like a singular in not being multiplied with its supposits: Father and Son are one God, whereas Socrates and Plato are several men. So its affirmation and negation are contradictory, and 'God generates' and 'God does not generate' cannot both be true.
claims: 'Deus' has features of both universal and singular terms.
Because 'Deus' is not multiplied with its supposits, 'God generates' and 'God does not generate' are contradictory.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e216.summary: First objection, that God begot either himself as God or another God. Same and other divide being universally; 'himself' (se) is a relative of identity and 'other' (alius) implies diversity.
claims: Same and other divide all being.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e219.summary: Second objection. 'God' is drawn to stand for a person by a notional adjunct, and 'other' implies notional distinction. Since 'God begot another divine person' is true, so is 'God begot another God'.
claims: 'Other' as a notional adjunct makes 'God' stand for a person.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e222.summary: Third objection, that 'God begot himself as God' is true. 'Same' is unity in substance as 'equal' is unity in quantity (the Philosopher). Father and Son have one magnitude and one substance, so as 'God begot an equal God' is granted, so should 'God begot the same God', and likewise 'himself as God'.
claims: Identity is unity in substance as equality is unity in quantity.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e226.summary: Fourth objection, on 'He begot God who is God the Father' and its negation. The affirmative seems false: the relative 'who' refers to the supposit of its antecedent, which stands for the Son, and 'the Son is God the Father' is false.
claims: The relative pronoun refers back to the supposit of its antecedent.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e229.summary: Fifth objection, that the negative is also false. Negation bears on the following term formally, so 'who is not God the Father' would remove 'God' from the Son as to form, not just supposit, removing the divine essence from the Son.
claims: Negation removes the form signified by the following term.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e232.summary: Thomas's determination. Lombard denies both 'he begot himself as God' and 'he begot another God'. 'Other', an adjective, places its diversity on the form of the term it modifies, implying a diversity of divinity. 'Himself', a relative of identity, refers to the same supposit, implying no distinction of supposits between Father and Son. Both must be denied. Some distinguish 'another God' as substantival (then appositive and true: 'another, who is God') or adjectival (false). But masculine adjectives are not normally substantivized, especially next to a noun, and supplying 'being' (alium entem Deum) is too forced. So with Lombard both are false.
claims: 'God begot another God' is false because 'other' implies diversity of nature.
'God begot himself as God' is false because 'himself' implies identity of supposit.
The substantival reading of 'alium' is too forced to rescue the proposition.
concepts: diversity of nature vs. of supposit

ta-l1d4q1-d1e235.summary: Reply to the first objection. Same and other suffice to divide created being, because in creatures diversity of supposits always means diversity of essence. In God there is one essence in diverse supposits, so neither identity fits (given the diverse supposits) nor diversity (given the one essence), only unity.
claims: In God, with one essence in several supposits, neither 'same' nor 'other' applies, only 'one'.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e238.summary: Reply to the second objection. 'Other' implies distinction in general, no more personal than essential. Joined to a personal term it implies personal distinction; joined to an essential term it implies diversity of essence, as the form of that term requires, since terms, especially substantial ones, receive diversity and plurality from their form.
claims: 'Other' takes its kind of distinction from the form of the term it modifies.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the third objection. 'Same' signifies unity in substance but, as a relative with implicit articulation, also implies unity of supposit, all the more so the reciprocal pronoun 'himself'. 'Equal' has no such feature, so the parallel fails.
claims: 'Same' and 'himself' imply unity of supposit, unlike 'equal'.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e245.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Lombard distinguishes both propositions. If 'Father' is construed appositively with 'God' ('he begot God, who is himself the Father'), the affirmative is false and the negative true. If the terms are joined mediately ('he begot God who is God, and God is the Father'), the affirmative is true and the negative false. Praepositinus held both false and not contradictory, because the relative refers only to the supposit in affirmatives but to supposit and essence in negatives. Thomas prefers Lombard's way: the distinction still applies, and there is no need for the relative to refer differently in negatives (negation confuses only the following term, not the preceding one). So each proposition can be true or false.
claims: Lombard's distinction between appositive and mediate construal resolves the propositions.
Praepositinus's view that relatives refer differently in negative propositions is rejected.

ta-l1d4q1-d1e251.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. When two terms are joined by apposition, the appositive term becomes like a form of the other. So on the appositive reading of 'he begot God who is not God the Father', the negation removes paternity, not divinity, from the Son.
claims: In apposition the added term functions as the form, so negation removes paternity rather than deity.

ta-l1d4q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 4 places Lombard's incidental questions on procession, first as to supposit and terminus and then as to principle, and frames the issue of whether essential names, concrete and abstract, can stand as supposit or terminus of generation. It announces inquiries into divine generation and divine predication.

ta-l1d4q1-Dd1e116.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is generation in God. Objections cite generation as change, its absence from the noblest creatures, the composition of the generated, and generation as a medium. Thomas holds generation in God on faith, not by proof. He explains that a name is said properly of God when imposed from a perfection, according to its constitutive difference, with the imperfection of its genus removed. Generation's genus (change, potency, division of essence) is excluded, but its difference, the communication and reception of nature in perfect likeness, is found first in God, and all creaturely generation imitates it. The replies call divine generation an operation, not a motion. Creatures generate imperfectly because their essence and esse differ. The Son differs from the Father only by relation, without composition, and generation is really paternity or filiation signified as act.
claims: There is generation in God, held by faith.
Generation as communication of nature in perfect likeness is primarily divine; creaturely generation imitates it.
Divine generation involves no change, composition, or intermediary.

ta-l1d4q1-Dd1e168.summary: Article 2 asks whether 'God begot God' is true. Objections argue that it implies God is distinct from God, that 'God' supposits for the essence, and that it would yield contradictions. Against them stand the Creed and the meaning 'one having deity'. Thomas holds the proposition simply true. Of two opinions he prefers the view that 'God' signifies the essence but of itself supposits indistinctly for a person, as a concrete name signifying by way of the subsistent. He explains the use of both abstract and concrete names for God. The replies show that notional verbs, being acts, require supposits, while 'distinguished' does not. The subject stands for the Father and the predicate for the Son, and 'God' is partly universal and partly singular, so 'God generates' and 'God does not generate' are contradictory.
claims: 'God begot God' is simply true.
'Deus' of itself supposits indistinctly for a person.
'Deus' is neither strictly universal nor singular.

ta-l1d4q1-Dd1e208.summary: Article 3 asks about related locutions. Following Lombard, Thomas rejects both 'God begot another God' (adjectival 'other' implies diversity of nature) and 'God begot himself as God' (reciprocal 'himself' implies identity of supposit). He dismisses a substantival reading of 'other' as forced. Same and other divide created being but not God, in whom there is unity without identity of supposits or diversity of essence. 'Other' takes its kind of distinction from the form of the term it modifies. For 'he begot God who is (not) God the Father', Thomas adopts Lombard's distinction between appositive and mediate construals over Praepositinus's view, so that each proposition is true or false according to the construal.
claims: 'God begot another God' and 'God begot himself as God' are both false.
Propositions with 'who is God the Father' are true or false according to appositive or mediate construal.

ta-l1d4q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 4 treats divine generation and the logic of essential names in notional propositions. Article 1 affirms, on faith, generation in God as the communication of nature in perfect likeness, removing the imperfections of the creaturely genus (change, potency, division). It also states a general rule: a name is said properly of God according to its constitutive difference, with generic imperfection removed. Article 2 defends 'God begot God' as simply true, on the view that 'Deus', as a concrete name, signifies the essence while of itself suppositing indistinctly for a person. Article 3 rejects 'God begot another God' and 'God begot himself as God' and resolves relative-clause propositions by Lombard's distinction between appositive and mediate construal. Throughout, Thomas uses supposition theory and the semantics of abstract and concrete names to keep both the unity of essence and the distinction of persons.
claims: There is generation in God, understood as communication of the same nature without change or composition.
'Deus' signifies the essence but supposits of itself indistinctly for a person, so 'God begot God' is true.
'God begot another God' and 'God begot himself as God' are false.
